name: Saab Sonett II
hook: Saab's first production sports car ran on a smoky two-stroke, and lost that engine within a year of going on sale.
story:
In early 1965, Saab held a little contest. Two prototypes rolled into Trollhättan.

One came from Sixten Sason, the man who had shaped Saab's sedans. The other came from Björn Karlström, who worked at an aircraft firm called MFI. Within a few weeks, Saab picked the aircraft man's car.

It went on sale at the end of 1966 as the Sonett II. A fibreglass body. A steel box frame with a roll bar built in. And the rally engine from the Monte Carlo 850: three cylinders, two strokes, 841 cc.

It was built to race, and in America it ran with Sprites and Spitfires. But the rules wanted 500 cars, and Saab had built 28 that first year.

Then the clean-air laws arrived. Two-strokes mixed oil into their fuel and smoked like a chimney. In the middle of 1967, Saab swapped in a Ford V4.

Only 258 two-stroke Sonetts were built. They were the last two-stroke sports cars Saab ever sold.
description: The Sonett II was Saab's first production sports car, built in Trollhättan, Sweden, from late 1966. It grew from the MFI13 prototype, designed by Björn Karlström. A fibreglass coupé body sat on a steel box chassis with an integral roll bar. Power came from the 841 cc three-cylinder two-stroke of the Saab Monte Carlo 850, driving the front wheels through a four-speed column shift. Only 258 were built before a Ford Taunus V4 replaced the two-stroke in 1967.
